title: Trigonometry
source: Barnett, Ziegler & Byleen, Analytic Trigonometry with Applications, 11th ed.; additions from Axler and Stewart

children.title: Why is a full turn 360°?
children.summary: Works through four stacked views (spec below)
children.spec:
The page stacksfour views, each answering "why not something else?":

1. **Divisibility:** a slider splits the circle into n equal slices. With 360, slices come out in whole degrees for 24 different n (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12…). A 100-unit circle manages only 9, and the 400-gradian circle 15. The student sees 360 win.
2. **The hexagon:** six radius-length chords close up exactly around any circle, giving six equilateral triangles. Babylonian base-60 makes each one 60, and 6 × 60 = 360.
3. **The sky:** the Sun shifts about 1° a day against the stars over a year of about 365 days, and early calendars rounded that to 360.
4. **It's a convention:** the same angle is shown as degrees, gradians, turns and radians. The geometry never changes; only the label does. This is the hand-off to radians.

Label views 2–3 honestly as the most widely accepted historical explanation, not a proven fact. View 1 is pure maths and always holds.

children.title: What is an angle, really?
children.summary: Spins the terminal ray past 360° and clockwise; a counter tracks revolutions, and coterminal angles show as ghosts

children.title: Why 60 minutes in a degree?
children.summary: Zooms into a 1° wedge that splits into 60 parts, then 60 again, beside a clock showing h:m:s (the book's marathon Explore/Discuss)

children.title: Why radians are the natural unit
children.summary: Wraps a radius-length string around a circle: it fits about 6.28 times, and still does after resizing the circle, so 1 rad ≈ 57.3°

children.title: Why does s = rθ only work in radians?
children.summary: Changes r and θ to watch the arc grow; switching to degrees breaks the formula unless π/180 sneaks in

children.title: Why is sector area ½r²θ?
children.summary: Slices a sector into thin triangles and rearranges them; the sector is the fraction θ/2π of the disc

children.title: Why arc ≈ chord for small angles
children.summary: Shrinks the angle and watches arc and chord merge; this sets up the Sun/Moon tool

children.title: Why does the outer horse go faster? (v = rω)
children.summary: Sees a merry-go-round where every rider has the same ω but the outer riders cover more arc per second

children.title: Angle unit lab: DMS ↔ DD ↔ radians
children.summary: Converts with a dual-scale protractor; also classifies acute/right/obtuse and complementary/supplementary pairs

children.title: Belts, gears and bicycle wheels
children.summary: Links two pulleys: the belt carries one linear speed, so the angular speeds differ

children.title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
children.summary: Sets the shadow angle at Alexandria and the distance to Syene, then reads off Earth's circumference

children.title: How big are the Sun and the Moon?
children.summary: Sets angular size and distance to get the diameter; both subtend about 0.5°, which is why total eclipses work

children.title: Why do a triangle's angles add to 180°?
children.summary: Drags vertices anywhere; the three corners tear off and line up on a straight line (and a parallel-line proof)

children.title: Why do same-shaped triangles have proportional sides?
children.summary: Scales a triangle with its angles locked while a live table of side ratios stays frozen (Euclid's theorem)

children.title: Why are two angles enough?
children.summary: Fixes two angles, tries to build a differently shaped triangle, and finds it can't, because the third angle is forced

children.title: Why does the ratio depend only on the angle?
children.summary: Fixes θ and resizes the right triangle: opp/hyp never moves. Changing θ changes it, so the ratio is a function of θ. This is the bridge into Box 3

children.title: Missing side by proportion
children.summary: Matches corresponding sides with colour coding and solves the proportion

children.title: Measure a tree with its shadow
children.summary: Moves a stick and the Sun; similar shadow triangles give the height (Thales)

children.title: How deep is a lunar crater?
children.summary: Uses the shadow length and Sun angle on the Moon to find the rim height (book exercise)

children.title: Why is a² + b² = c²?
children.summary: Drags a slider that rearranges four copies of the triangle inside a square; the leftover area is c² or a² + b²

children.title: Why exactly six ratios?
children.summary: Picks 2 of the 3 sides in order and finds 6 combinations, in 3 reciprocal pairs

children.title: Why is it called "co"-sine?
children.summary: Switches the viewpoint to the other acute angle: opposite and adjacent swap, so cos θ = sin(90° − θ)

children.title: Why do sin and cos stay ≤ 1 while tan doesn't?
children.summary: Pushes θ toward 90°: the hypotenuse is always longest, but tan blows up

children.title: Where does the calculator's 0.6018 come from?
children.summary: Measures a huge drawn 37° triangle and compares the ratio with the calculator

children.title: Why is it called 'sine'?
children.summary: Traces the word from Aryabhata's jyā/jīvā (half-chord) to Arabic jība, misread as jaib ('fold') and translated into Latin as sinus

children.title: Solve a right triangle
children.summary: Enters any two parts and gets a step-by-step solution, with the triangle highlighting which ratio is used

children.title: How accurate is my answer?
children.summary: Sees how the precision of an angle pairs with the significant digits of the sides (the book's accuracy table)

children.title: Angles of elevation and depression
children.summary: Walks an observer toward a building and reads its height off the angle

children.title: Height from two sightings
children.summary: Takes angles from two points and finds the height without reaching the base (the book's 4.8 + x problem)

children.title: Why does light bend? (refraction)
children.summary: Moves the incoming ray and changes the material; sin α / sin β stays constant (Snell's law)

children.title: Why is a wake V-shaped?
children.summary: Uses one cone tool with three presets, boat bow wave, sonic boom and Čerenkov light, all following sin(θ/2) = slow speed / fast speed

children.title: Why do we need a circle at all?
children.summary: Pushes a right triangle past 90° until it collapses; switches to point (x, y) on a circle of radius r, where x/r and y/r agree with the triangle for acute angles and keep working beyond

children.title: Why radius 1?
children.summary: Resizes the circle: the ratios don't change, and at r = 1 the coordinates simply are (cos θ, sin θ)

children.title: Why do signs change by quadrant?
children.summary: Drags the point around and watches the signs of x and y; ASTC falls out of this, with nothing to memorise

children.title: Why do reference angles work?
children.summary: Mirrors a Q2/Q3/Q4 point into Q1: the same lengths with different signs

children.title: Why is sin 30° exactly ½?
children.summary: Halves an equilateral triangle to get 30–60–90, cuts a square on its diagonal to get 45–45–90, and reads off the exact values

children.title: Why sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
children.summary: Sees Pythagoras on the radius of the unit circle, true at every angle

children.title: Why do trig functions repeat?
children.summary: Winds around several times: coterminal angles land on the same point, so the period is 2π; tan repeats every π because opposite points give the same slope

children.title: Why is tan 90° undefined?
children.summary: Moves the point to (0, 1), where y/x divides by zero; the nearby values shoot off to ±∞

children.title: Why is sine a function (and the circle isn't)?
children.summary: Feeds angles into a machine: one input gives exactly one output, but one x gives two points on the circle

children.title: Why is cos even and sin odd?
children.summary: Mirrors the point across the x-axis: x stays the same and y flips

children.title: Exact-value drill
children.summary: Clicks a special or quadrantal angle and fills in all six values, with the triangle shown as a hint

children.title: Degree mode vs radian mode
children.summary: Sees the same keystrokes give different answers; spots the classic sin(30) = −0.988 mistake

children.title: Why is the sine graph a wave?
children.summary: Watches a point spin on the unit circle while its height is traced onto a time axis beside it. This is the signature visual of the site

children.title: Why is cosine a shifted sine?
children.summary: Traces the horizontal shadow of the same spinner: it's sine started a quarter-turn early

children.title: What does A do? Amplitude = radius
children.summary: Grows the circle and the wave grows taller with it

children.title: What does B do? Why period = 2π/B
children.summary: Spins B times faster, so one full turn takes 2π/B

children.title: What does C do? Why the shift is −C/B
children.summary: Starts the spinner early by angle C and sees why the graph shifts left, and why the shift divides by B

children.title: What does k do?
children.summary: Lifts the axle and the whole wave rises with it

children.title: Transformation lab for any graph
children.summary: Applies shifts, reflections and stretches to any f(x) and sees A, B, C, k as one general idea

children.title: Graph y = k + A sin(Bx + C) by hand
children.summary: Gets the five key points step by step, then checks against the live plot

children.title: Find the equation from a graph
children.summary: Drags a sine curve to fit a target graph, then writes its equation (simple harmonic)

children.title: Why does the graph window matter?
children.summary: Zooms a plotter out until the samples skip cycles and a fake wave appears (aliasing)

children.title: Why do tilted lines fool your eyes?
children.summary: Tilts a field of lines and plots the error d = a + b sin 4θ; the period is 90° because the pattern looks the same after a quarter-turn (Berliner experiment)

children.title: Fit a sine to real data
children.summary: Fits y = A sin(ωx − φ) + B to daylight hours or monthly temperatures

children.title: Why is it called "tangent"?
children.summary: Sees tan θ is the length of the tangent line at (1, 0) and sec θ the length of the secant line out to it, so the names are literal

children.title: Why does tan have asymptotes?
children.summary: Pushes θ toward 90°: the ray becomes parallel to the tangent line and the segment runs off forever

children.title: tan θ is a slope
children.summary: Rotates a ray and reads its slope, which equals tan θ; that's why the period is π

children.title: Why is cot the "co"-tangent?
children.summary: Uses the tangent line at (0, 1) instead: the complementary angle and the mirror-image graph

children.title: Why do csc and sec hug sin and cos?
children.summary: Overlays the reciprocals: where sin → 0, csc → ∞, and where sin = ±1 they touch, which makes the U-shapes

children.title: Graph y = A tan(Bx + C) and A cot(Bx + C)
children.summary: Places the asymptotes π/B apart first, then the curve between them

children.title: Graph y = A sec(Bx + C) and A csc(Bx + C)
children.summary: Draws the guide sine/cosine faintly, then flips it into U-shapes

children.title: Why is there no amplitude for tan?
children.summary: Tries to measure a peak height and finds none; A becomes a vertical stretch

children.title: Lighthouse beam on a wall
children.summary: Rotates the beam steadily and sees the spot's position (d tan θ) and its speed explode near 90°

children.title: Why does a spring trace a sine?
children.summary: Runs a spinning point and a mass on a spring side by side: the mass is the point's shadow (simple harmonic motion)

children.title: Why do waves add point by point?
children.summary: Drags two waves and watches a vertical line add their heights at each x (addition of ordinates)

children.title: Why do beats happen?
children.summary: Tunes two close frequencies and sees and hears the loud–soft envelope; the product–sum identity explains it

children.title: Why does damping make an envelope?
children.summary: Multiplies the sine by a decaying curve and sees the curve become the boundary

children.title: Why does resonance build up?
children.summary: Sweeps the drive frequency past the natural frequency and watches the amplitude spike

children.title: Why is any shape a sum of sines?
children.summary: Adds harmonics one by one and watches a square or sawtooth wave assemble (Fourier)

children.title: Pitch = 1 / period
children.summary: Changes B and hears the tone change (Web Audio) with the graph locked to it

children.title: Weigh a floating object by its bobbing
children.summary: Sets the mass and area and times the period, then inverts to find the mass

children.title: Why 120π in AC current?
children.summary: Reads 60 cycles per second off the graph of I = A sin 120πt

children.title: Light and EM waves: c = λf
children.summary: Slides across the spectrum; wavelength and frequency trade off at constant speed

children.title: Water waves
children.summary: Changes wavelength and period and sees the wave speed

children.title: Coyotes and rabbits
children.summary: Watches two population sines run a quarter-cycle apart; predators lag prey

children.title: Why three Pythagorean identities?
children.summary: Scales the unit-circle triangle by 1/cos and by 1/sin to get 1 + tan² = sec² and 1 + cot² = csc², the same triangle resized

children.title: Identity vs equation: true everywhere or somewhere?
children.summary: Graphs both sides: an identity overlaps everywhere, an equation only crosses at points

children.title: Why cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B
children.summary: Rotates a chord around the unit circle; its length is the same both ways, which gives the identity

children.title: Why sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B
children.summary: Stacks one triangle on another inside a rectangle; the side lengths read off the identity

children.title: Why isn't sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B?
children.summary: Drags A and B and watches the two bars disagree, with a live counterexample

children.title: Why double-angle formulas?
children.summary: Sets B = A in the sum formula, then checks with an isosceles triangle in a circle

children.title: Why do half-angle formulas have ±?
children.summary: Moves θ around and sees which quadrant θ/2 lands in, which picks the sign

children.title: Why can products become sums?
children.summary: Adds two spinning phasors; their sum and difference frequencies appear (links to beats)

children.title: Why is M sin Bt + N cos Bt a single sine?
children.summary: Adds two perpendicular phasors: the resultant has length √(M² + N²) and a phase angle

children.title: Why is arccos t + arcsin t = π/2?
children.summary: Sees that in a right triangle the two acute angles are complementary

children.title: Identity verifier sandbox
children.summary: Transforms one side step by step while a graph confirms that every step stays equal

children.title: All six from one
children.summary: Given sin θ = 3/5 in Q2, draws the triangle in that quadrant and reads off the rest

children.title: Why can't sine be inverted as it is?
children.summary: Sweeps a horizontal line across the wave: it hits many times, so sine is not one-to-one

children.title: Why those exact ranges for arcsin and arccos?
children.summary: Slides a window along the graph; only some windows are one-to-one, cover −1…1, are unbroken, and include 0 to π/2

children.title: Why is an inverse graph a mirror image?
children.summary: Folds the graph over y = x

children.title: Why does sin x = 0.5 have infinitely many solutions?
children.summary: Sees the line cross the wave again and again; the unit circle shows two per turn, plus 2πk

children.title: Why sin(sin⁻¹ x) = x but sin⁻¹(sin x) ≠ x
children.summary: Chains the two machines and sees outputs fold back once x leaves the range

children.title: Why do books disagree on arcsec's range?
children.summary: Compares the two common branch choices side by side

children.title: What happens to sin(1/x) near 0?
children.summary: Zooms in forever and finds more and more solutions

children.title: Why is sin(cos⁻¹ x) = √(1 − x²)?
children.summary: Draws the triangle that cos⁻¹ x describes and reads the sine off it

children.title: Solve a trig equation
children.summary: Isolates the function, finds the reference angle, picks every quadrant, writes the general solution

children.title: Solve graphically, including inequalities
children.summary: Finds intersections, then shades where f > g

children.title: Inverse and composition drill
children.summary: Evaluates sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ and their compositions, with the answer drawn on the circle

children.title: Solve a sin x + b cos x = c
children.summary: Rewrites the left side as a single sine, then solves

children.title: Why the law of sines?
children.summary: Drops an altitude: h = b sin A = a sin B, and the law follows

children.title: Why a/sin A = 2R
children.summary: Draws the circumcircle and sees every ratio equal its diameter

children.title: Why is SSA ambiguous?
children.summary: Swings side a like a compass arc that crosses the base 0, 1 or 2 times

children.title: Why is the law of cosines Pythagoras with a correction?
children.summary: Opens the right angle; the −2ab cos C term grows and shrinks with it

children.title: Why does SSS fix a triangle but AAA doesn't?
children.summary: Three rods make a rigid frame, while three angles still allow any size

children.title: Why is area ½ab sin C?
children.summary: Sees the height is b sin C, so ½ × base × height becomes ½ab sin C

children.title: Why does Heron's formula follow from the law of cosines?
children.summary: Substitutes cos C into ½ab sin C and watches the algebra collapse

children.title: Why can two different triangles have the same area?
children.summary: Swaps angle θ for 180° − θ: sin is unchanged, so ½ab sin θ is too

children.title: Heron's formula check
children.summary: Drags vertices and compares ½ × base × height, ½ab sin C and Heron's formula live

children.title: Triangle solver: which law, and why?
children.summary: Picks the case (ASA, AAS, SSA, SAS, SSS) and is shown the law to use and the reason

children.title: Area of any polygon
children.summary: Splits a shape into triangles and sums them (the book's arbitrary-triangle method)

children.title: Distance across a river
children.summary: Sights a tree from two points on one bank and finds the width with the law of sines

children.title: Why does a vector need two numbers?
children.summary: Drags an arrow and sees magnitude + direction and components ⟨‖v‖ cos θ, ‖v‖ sin θ⟩ as two names for one thing

children.title: Why tip-to-tail?
children.summary: Walks one displacement, then another; the parallelogram gives the same result

children.title: Why does a scalar stretch but not turn a vector?
children.summary: Slides k from −2 to 2: the arrow stretches and flips, but stays on its line

children.title: Why is u · v = ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ?
children.summary: Casts u's shadow onto v; the law of cosines shows the algebraic and geometric forms agree

children.title: Why does perpendicular mean dot = 0?
children.summary: Rotates u around v and watches the shadow vanish at 90°

children.title: Why does the dot product come from complex numbers?
children.summary: Multiplies (a − bi)(c + di) and finds its real part is exactly ac + bd, the dot product

children.title: Unit vectors and direction
children.summary: Scales any vector to length 1 and back

children.title: Split a vector into parallel and perpendicular parts
children.summary: Projects one vector onto another and draws both components

children.title: Plane in a crosswind
children.summary: Sets heading, airspeed and wind; the ground track is the vector sum

children.title: Why do cable tensions explode as they flatten?
children.summary: Hangs a sign from two cables; as the angle closes in, the tension needed to hold the weight shoots up (static equilibrium)

children.title: Work when pulling at an angle
children.summary: Pulls a sled: only the component along the motion does work, W = F · d

children.title: Block on an incline
children.summary: Splits gravity into components along and across the slope (scalar component)

children.title: Why polar coordinates?
children.summary: Locates points radar-style (turn, then walk) and compares with x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ

children.title: Why does one point have many polar names?
children.summary: Adds 2π or flips to negative r and lands on the same dot

children.title: Why does a rose have n or 2n petals?
children.summary: Traces r = a cos nθ with a pen: for even n, negative r draws new petals behind; for odd n, it retraces

children.title: Polar curve gallery
children.summary: Moves sliders through cardioid, limaçon, spiral, lemniscate and rose (the book's table of standard curves)

children.title: Why does i live on a perpendicular axis?
children.summary: Multiplies by i repeatedly: each time is a 90° turn, so i² = −1 is a 180° turn

children.title: Why does multiplying complex numbers add angles?
children.summary: Multiplies two numbers and sees the lengths multiply and the angles add

children.title: Why De Moivre?
children.summary: Raises r∠θ to the n-th power: a spiral of n equal turns

children.title: Why are n roots evenly spaced?
children.summary: Drags n: the roots form a regular n-gon on a circle

children.title: Polar ↔ rectangular converter
children.summary: Converts points and equations both ways, with a dual grid

children.title: Complex arithmetic: rectangular vs polar
children.summary: Does the same product both ways and sees why polar is easier

children.title: Orbits of planets
children.summary: Changes the eccentricity in r = a(1 − e²)/(1 + e cos θ) to go from circle to ellipse
